en: Taittirīya Upaniṣad: Oṃ! May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious; may Aryaman be auspicious to us;
may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us.
Homage to Brahman!
Homage to you, O Vāyu!
You alone are the manifest Brahman.
I shall speak of you alone as manifest Brahman;
I shall speak the Ṛta;
I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me;
may it protect the speaker;
may it protect me, and may it protect the speaker.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace. 1.1.1.
Thus ends the first section.
Oṃ. We shall explain phonetics (śīkṣā). [It consists of: the letter, the accent, the measure, the strength, the melody, and the continuity. Thus has been stated the chapter on phonetics. 1.2.1.
Thus ends the second section.

May glory be ours together; may spiritual splendor be ours together. Now, therefore, we shall explain the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the *Saṃhitā* in five sections: concerning the worlds (*adhiloka*), concerning the luminaries (*adhijyautiṣa*), concerning knowledge (*adhividyā*), concerning progeny (*adhipraja*), and concerning the self (*adhyātma*). These are called the "Great *Saṃhitās*. Now, concerning the worlds: the earth is the prior form; the sky is the posterior form; space is the junction (*sandhi*); and the wind is the connection (*saṃdhāna*). This is concerning the worlds. Now, concerning the luminaries: fire is the prior form; the sun is the posterior form; the waters are the junction; and lightning is the connection. This is concerning the luminaries. Now, concerning knowledge: the teacher is the prior form; the pupil is the posterior form; knowledge is the junction; and instruction is the connection. This is concerning knowledge. Now, concerning progeny: the mother is the prior form; the father is the posterior form; offspring is the junction; and procreation is the connection. This is concerning progeny. Now, concerning the self: the lower jaw is the prior form; the upper jaw is the posterior form; speech is the junction; and the tongue is the connection. This is concerning the self. These are the Great *Saṃhitās*. Whoever knows these Great *Saṃhitās* as they have been explained is joined with offspring, with cattle, with spiritual splendor, with food, and with the heavenly world.
Thus ends the third section.
May he who is the bull among the meters, the omniform, who was born from the nectar of the meters—may that Indra strengthen me with wisdom; O God, may I become a vessel for the nectar of immortality.
May my body be radiant; may my tongue be most sweet;
may I hear much with my two ears.
You are the treasury of Brahman, covered by wisdom; protect what I have heard.
Bringing, spreading out,
and quickly providing for herself garments, cows, and food and drink for me at all times—
from that, bring prosperity to me, together with hairy livestock; *svāhā*.
May the students of sacred knowledge come to me; Svāhā!
May the students of sacred knowledge go forth from me; Svāhā!
May the students of sacred knowledge advance toward me; Svāhā!
May the students of sacred knowledge be subdued, svāhā! May the students of sacred knowledge be pacified, svāhā! 1.4.2.
May I be glorious among the people, svāhā!
May I be better than the wealthy, svāhā!
O Bhaga, may I enter into you, svāhā!
O Bhaga, enter me, svāhā!
In you, who have a thousand branches, O Bhaga, I cleanse myself, svāhā!
Just as waters flow down a slope, just as months follow the passing of days.
Thus may the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) come toward me from all sides, O Ordainer; svāhā! You are my neighbor; shine upon me; come to me. 1.4.3.
Thus ends the fourth section.

"Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ"—these are indeed the three *vyāhṛtis*. Of these, Māhācamasya used to proclaim a fourth: "Mahaḥ. That is Brahman; that is the Self (*ātman*); the other deities are its limbs. "Bhūr" is this world; "bhuvaḥ" is the intermediate space; "suvaḥ" is yonder world. "Mahaḥ" is the sun; by the sun, indeed, all worlds are magnified (*mahīyante*). "Bhūr" is Agni; "bhuvaḥ" is Vāyu; "suvaḥ" is Āditya; "mahaḥ" is the moon. By the moon, indeed, all luminaries are magnified. "Bhūr" is the *ṛc*s; "bhuvaḥ" is the *sāmans*; "suvaḥ" is the *yajus*s. "Mahaḥ" is Brahman; by Brahman, indeed, all the Vedas are magnified. "Bhūr" is the out-breath (*prāṇa*); "bhuvaḥ" is the in-breath (*apāna*); "suvaḥ" is the diffused breath (*vyāna*); "mahaḥ" is food. By food, indeed, all vital breaths are magnified. These four *vyāhṛtis* are thus fourfold—four each. He who knows them knows Brahman; all the gods bring him tribute.
Thus ends the fifth section.

That which is this space within the heart—in it is this person consisting of mind, immortal and golden. Between the two palates is that which hangs down like a nipple; that is the birthplace of Indra. Having parted the two halves of the skull, [the syllables] *bhūḥ* establishes itself in fire, *bhuvaḥ* in wind, *suvar* in the sun, and *mahaḥ* in Brahman. He attains self-sovereignty; he attains the Lord of Mind. He becomes the Lord of Speech, the Lord of Sight, the Lord of Hearing, and the Lord of Discernment. This is what results from that: Brahman has space as its body, truth as its self, life-breath as its delight, and the mind as its bliss; it is rich in peace and immortal. Thus, O Prācīnayogya, do thou worship.
Thus ends the sixth section.

Earth, the intermediate space, heaven, the quarters, and the intermediate directions; fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars; water, herbs, trees, space, and the self—this is with respect to the elements (adhibhūta).

Now, with reference to the self: the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the in-breath (*apāna*), the upward breath (*udāna*), and the equalizing breath (*samāna*); the eye, the ear, the mind, speech, and the skin; the skin, the flesh, the sinews, the bone, and the marrow. Having analyzed this, the seer said: "All this is fivefold; by means of the fivefold, one gains the fivefold. 1.7.1.
Thus ends the seventh section.

"Om" is Brahman. "Om," this whole world is. Indeed, even when they say, "Make them hear! they cause them to hear with "Om. They sing the Sāmans with "Om. They recite the Śastras with "Oṃ śom. The Adhvaryu priest responds with the Pratigara with "Om. The Brahmā priest gives the command with "Om. One authorizes the Agnihotra sacrifice with "Om. A Brāhmaṇa, about to speak, says, "May I attain Brahman," and he indeed attains Brahman. 1.8.1.
Thus ends the eighth section.

The sacred law (*ṛta*) and study and teaching; truth (*satya*) and study and teaching; austerity (*tapas*) and study and teaching; self-restraint (*dama*) and study and teaching; tranquility (*śama*) and study and teaching; the sacred fires (*agni*) and study and teaching; the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) and study and teaching; guests (*atithi*) and study and teaching; human duties (*mānuṣa*) and study and teaching; progeny (*prajā*) and study and teaching; procreation (*prajana*) and study and teaching; and offspring (*prajāti*) and study and teaching. "Truth," says Satyavacas Rāthītara. "Austerity," says Taponitya Pauruśiṣṭi. "Only study and teaching," says Nāka Maudgalya; for that indeed is austerity, that indeed is austerity. 1.9.1.
Thus ends the ninth section.

I am like the swiftness of a tree; my fame is like the ridge of a mountain. With my purifier raised high, like a prize-winning steed, I am my own immortal wealth, full of splendor, wise, immortal, and inexhaustible.
Thus ends the recitation of the Vedas by Triśaṅku. 1.10.1.
Thus ends the tenth section.

Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil: "Speak the truth. Practice righteousness. Do not neglect your private Vedic study. Having brought wealth that is pleasing to your teacher, do not let the thread of progeny be cut off. One must not swerve from the truth. One must not swerve from righteousness. One must not swerve from what is beneficial. One must not swerve from prosperity. One must not swerve from private study and the recitation [of the Veda]. (1.11.1) One must not swerve from the rites for the gods and the ancestors. Be one to whom the mother is a god; be one to whom the father is a god; be one to whom the teacher is a god; be one to whom the guest is a god. Those actions which are blameless—those should be practiced by you, and not others. Those good deeds of ours—those should be emulated by you, and not others. Whatever Brahmins there may be who are more distinguished than we, you should offer them a seat. One should give with faith; one should give without faith. One should give with dignity; one should give with modesty. One should give with fear; one should give with a sense of obligation. Now, if you should have any doubt regarding a ritual act or a course of conduct, (1.11.3) those Brahmins there who are reflective, disciplined, unworldly, and lovers of righteousness—just as they would behave in that situation, so should you behave. And in the case of those who are accused, those Brahmins there who are reflective, disciplined, unworldly, and lovers of righteousness—just as they would behave toward them, so should you behave toward them. This is the injunction; this is the instruction; this is the secret doctrine of the Veda (*vedopaniṣad*); this is the precept. Thus should it be observed; and thus indeed should it be observed. (1.11.4)
Thus ends the eleventh section.
May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious, and may Aryaman be auspicious to us.
May Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us.
Homage to Brahman! Homage to you, O Vāyu!
You alone are the perceptible Brahman. To you alone as the perceptible Brahman have I spoken;
I have spoken the *ṛta*; I have spoken the truth.
That protected me; that protected the speaker. It has protected me; it has protected the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace. 1.12.1.
Thus ends the twelfth section.
The Chapter on Training: The First Creeper. Om!
May He protect us both together.
May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work together with vigor;
may our study be brilliant; may we never harbor enmity toward one another.
Oṃ,
peace, peace, peace.

The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Regarding this, the following verse has been sung: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. He who knows that which is hidden in the secret cave of the heart, in the highest heaven—he attains all desires together with the omniscient Brahman."

From this very Self, indeed, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, man. This person, indeed, consists of the essence of food. Of him, this is the head; this is the right wing; this is the left wing; this is the trunk; this is the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse: 2.1.1.
Thus ends the first section.
From food indeed are creatures born, whatever dwell upon the earth;
moreover, by food alone they live, and into it they finally pass away.
For food is the eldest of all beings; therefore it is called the universal medicine.
Indeed, all food reaches those who worship food as Brahman.
For food is the eldest of all beings; therefore, it is called the universal medicine.
"From food beings are born; once born, they grow by means of food. It is eaten, and it eats beings; therefore it is called 'food' (anna). Thus it is said.

Now, different from this self consisting of the essence of food is another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). By that, this [self] is filled. That very one is indeed of the form of a person. Following its person-like form, it is person-like. Of that, breath itself is the head; the *vyāna* is the right wing; the *apāna* is the left wing; space is the trunk; and the earth is the tail, the support. On this point there is also this verse: 2.2.1.
Thus ends the second section.
The gods breathe after the vital breath (prāṇa), as do humans and animals;
for the vital breath is the life-span of all beings, and therefore it is called "all-encompassing life."
"Those who meditate upon *prāṇa* as Brahman attain their full span of life;
for *prāṇa* is the life-force (*āyus*) of all beings, therefore it is called 'all-encompassing life' (*sarvāyuṣa*).
This very one is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of that [previous one]. It is the same as that of the former.

Now, different from this self consisting of breath is another inner self consisting of mind; by that [self] this one is filled. That very self is indeed of the form of a person. Following its person-like form, it is person-like. Of that [self], the Yajus is the head; the Ṛk is the right wing; the Sāman is the left wing; the Instruction (Ādeśa) is the trunk; and the Atharva-Āṅgirases are the tail, the support. On this point there is also this verse: 2.3.1.
Thus ends the third section.
"From which words turn back, along with the mind, not having attained it—
he who knows that bliss of Brahman fears nothing at any time.
This very one is the embodied self of that [previous Brahman], which belongs to the former.

Now, different from this self consisting of mind is the inner self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). By it this [self] is filled. That very one is indeed of the form of a person. Following its person-like form, it is of the form of a person. Faith is its head; truth is its right wing; reality is its left wing; meditation (*yoga*) is its trunk; greatness (*mahaḥ*) is its tail, the support. On this point there is also this verse: 2.4.1.1.105–106 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * **Faith** (*śraddhā*) is the head, for it is the foremost. * **Truth** (*ṛta*) is the right wing, representing the cosmic order of the sacrificial ritual. * **Reality** (*satya*) is the left wing, representing the cosmic order of the natural world. * **Yoga** is the trunk (*ātman*), the central body, signifying the integration of the individual with the divine. * **Greatness** (*mahaḥ*) is the tail, the foundation, representing the vast expanse of the Absolute. On this subject, there is also the following verse: 2.4.1.107–108 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "The self consisting of consciousness is surrounded on all sides by the self consisting of mind. One who knows this becomes a consumer of food and attains lordship over the mind. * "The self consisting of consciousness is surrounded on all sides by the self consisting of breath. One who knows this becomes a consumer of food and attains lordship over breath. 2.4.1.109–110 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "The self consisting of breath is surrounded on all sides by the self consisting of space. One who knows this becomes a consumer of food and attains lordship over space. * "The self consisting of space is surrounded on all sides by the self consisting of the immortal. One who knows this becomes a consumer of food and attains lordship over the immortal. 2.4.1.111–112 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "The self consisting of the immortal is surrounded on all sides by the self consisting of the infinite. One who knows this becomes a consumer of food and attains lordship over the infinite. * "The self consisting of the infinite is surrounded on all sides by the self consisting of bliss. One who knows this becomes a consumer of food and attains lordship over bliss. 2.4.1.113–114 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "That which is bliss is the Brahman of the blissful ones. For only when one finds rest in that Brahman does one become blissful. * "If one does not find rest in that Brahman, one becomes miserable. For only when one finds rest in that Brahman does one become blissful. 2.4.1.115–116 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "This is the Brahman of the blissful ones, wherein all desires have been fulfilled, which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, hungerless, thirstless, whose desire is the Self, and which is satisfied through the Self. * "Those who reach that world without having discovered it here, and those who do so after discovering it—both, upon departing from this world, enter into that very Self. 2.4.1.117–118 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "As rivers flowing towards the sea lose their names and forms upon reaching the sea, so too a wise man, freed from name and form, reaches the supreme, undecaying Self, which is higher than the high. * "He who realizes this becomes one with the light of the sun, rising above the heavens. He becomes the self of all beings; whatever he desires, he obtains. 2.4.1.119–120 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "This is the Brahman of the blissful ones, wherein all desires have been fulfilled, which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, hungerless, thirstless, whose desire is the Self, and which is satisfied through the Self. * "Those who depart from this world having realized this, they enter into these very worlds according to their desire. Those who depart without realizing this, they enter into these worlds according to their karma. 2.4.1.121–122 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "Now, regarding this, there is this verse: 'In the beginning, this was only the existent, one without a second. Some say it was the non-existent. * "From that, how could existence arise? How could the existent come from the non-existent? On the contrary, in the beginning, this was only the existent, one without a second. 2.4.1.123–124 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "It thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth. It emitted heat. That heat thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth. It emitted water. * "That water thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth. It emitted food. Regarding this, there is also this verse: 2.4.1.125–126 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "From the existent, the existent arose. Once the existent had arisen, it solidified into a mass of being. That became the earth, the atmosphere, and the sky. * "That became the ocean, the mountains, the rivers, and the various directions. Thus did the existent expand in various ways. 2.4.1.127–128 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "Whatever appeared as diverse, it was the existent alone. The wise perceive it as one; the ignorant perceive it as manifold. * "When a man departs from this world, he enters into the air. The air opens up for him like a chariot-way. Through it, he proceeds to the sun. 2.4.1.129–130 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "The sun opens up for him like a lotus-blossom. Through it, he proceeds to the world of Brahman. That is the highest world. That is the end. That is the final goal. * "Those who depart from this world having realized this, they enter into these very worlds according to their desire. Those who depart without realizing this, they enter into these worlds according to their karma. 2.4.1.131–132 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "Now, regarding this, there is this verse: 'In the beginning, this was only the existent, one without a second. Some say it was the non-existent. * "From that, how could existence arise? How could the existent come from the non-existent? On the contrary, in the beginning, this was only the existent, one without a second. 2.4.1.133–134 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "It thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth. It emitted heat. That heat thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth. It emitted water. * "That water thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth. It emitted food. Regarding this, there is also this verse: 2.4.1.135–136 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.1) * "From the existent, the existent arose. Once the existent had arisen, it solidified into
Thus ends the fourth section.
Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs ritual actions;
all the gods worship consciousness as the supreme Brahman.
"If one knows that consciousness is Brahman, and if one does not become negligent because of that,
then, having cast off all evils from the body, one enjoys all desires.
This very one is the embodied self of that [previous one], which belongs to the former.

Now, different from this self consisting of consciousness is another inner self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). By him this [self] is filled. He, indeed, is of the very form of a person (*puruṣavidha*). Following his being of the form of a person, he too is of the form of a person. His joy (*priya*) is the head; his delight (*moda*) is the right wing; his extreme delight (*pramoda*) is the left wing; bliss (*ānanda*) is the trunk (*ātman*); Brahman is the tail, the support. On this there is also this verse: 2.5.1
Thus ends the fifth section.
"If one knows Brahman as non-existent, he himself becomes non-existent;
but if one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as existing.
Of that [latter], this very same is the embodied self, which belongs to the former.
Now, therefore, follow these further questions:
Does anyone who is ignorant go to that world after departing? Or does someone who knows attain that world after departing?
Thus ends the sixth section.
"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, the existent was born.
It made itself by itself; therefore, it is called 'well-made' (sukṛta). Thus [it is said].

That which is indeed well-done is truly essence (*rasa*). For it is by obtaining essence alone that one becomes blissful. For who indeed could inhale, who could exhale, if this bliss were not present in this space? It is he alone who causes bliss. For when a person finds fearless support in that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and without abode, then he has become free from fear. But when he perceives even a slight difference in it, then fear arises for him. This very fear belongs to the one who thinks he knows [only partially]. On this there is also this verse: 2.7.1.1.105–106.108 (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1) *Note: The provided text contains the core philosophical argument regarding bliss (*ānanda*) as the essence of reality and the source of fearlessness, concluding with the transition to the famous verse on the "fear arising from perceiving difference. The numbering follows the standard Taittirīya Upaniṣad sequence.*
Thus ends the seventh section.
"From fear of him the wind blows; from fear of him the sun rises;
from fear of him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, speed along.

This is the inquiry into bliss. A man should be young, youthful, a student of the Vedas, most swift, most firm, and most strong. Suppose this entire earth were filled with his wealth; that is one human bliss.

A hundred human joys make up one joy of the human *gandharvas*, and of a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire. A hundred joys of the human *gandharvas* make up one joy of the divine *gandharvas*, and of a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire. A hundred joys of the divine *gandharvas* make up one joy of the ancestors who dwell in the long-lasting world (*ciraloka*), and of a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire.

A hundredfold the joys of the ancestors who dwell in the long-lasting worlds constitute one joy of the gods by birth (*ājānajāna*), and likewise of a learned man (*śrotriya*) who is unassailed by desire. A hundredfold the joys of the gods by birth constitute one joy of the gods by action (*karmadeva*), and likewise of a learned man who is unassailed by desire.
A hundredfold the joys of the gods by action constitute one joy of the gods, and likewise of a learned man who is unassailed by desire.

A hundred joys of the gods constitute one joy of Indra, and also of a learned Vedic scholar who is untouched by desire. A hundred joys of Indra constitute one joy of Bṛhaspati, and also of a learned Vedic scholar who is untouched by desire.
A hundred joys of Bṛhaspati constitute one joy of Prajāpati, and also of a learned Vedic scholar who is untouched by desire.
A hundred joys of Prajāpati are equal to one joy of Brahman, and also of a learned Śrotriya who is untouched by desire.

That which is in this person and that which is in yonder sun are one and the same. He who knows this, after departing from this world, passes into this self consisting of food, he passes into this self consisting of vital breath, he passes into this self consisting of mind, he passes into this self consisting of consciousness, and he passes into this self consisting of bliss. Regarding this, there is also this verse: 2.8.1
Thus ends the eighth section.

"From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—knowing that bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing from anywhere. Indeed, this does not afflict him: "Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is evil? He who knows thus protects both these worlds by protecting himself; for he who knows thus protects both of these by protecting himself. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 2.8.1.
Thus ends the ninth section.
Thus ends the Brahmavallī.
Oṃ!
May He protect us both; may He nourish us both;
may we work together with vigor.
May our study be luminous; may we not harbor mutual hatred. Om.
Peace, peace, peace.

Bhṛgu Vāruṇi indeed approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Venerable sir, teach me Brahman. He spoke this to him: "Food, breath, the eye, the ear, the mind, and speech. He said to him: "That from which these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which they enter at their passing—desire to know that; that is Brahman. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, [he realized it]. 3.1.1.
Thus ends the first section.

"Food is Brahman"—thus he understood. For indeed, from food alone these beings are born; once born, they live by food; and at death, they enter back into food. Having realized this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, O Venerable One. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, [he understood]. 3.2.1.
Thus ends the second section.

"He understood that *prāṇa* is Brahman; for indeed from *prāṇa* these beings are born, by *prāṇa* they live once born, and into *prāṇa* they enter at death. Having understood this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, venerable sir. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity (*tapas*); austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, [he understood]. 3.3.1.
Thus ends the third section.

"He understood that the mind is Brahman; for indeed from the mind alone these beings are born, by the mind, once born, they live, and into the mind they enter at their passing away. Having realized this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, O Venerable One. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, [he saw... 3.4.1.
Thus ends the fourth section.

"Consciousness is Brahman," he understood. "For indeed, from consciousness alone these beings are born; by consciousness, once born, they live; into consciousness they enter at death. Having understood this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, venerable sir. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity (*tapas*); austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, [he understood]. 3.5.1.
Thus ends the fifth section.

"Bliss is Brahman"—thus he understood. For indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; into bliss they enter at death and merge. This is that knowledge of Bhārgava and Vāruṇi, established in the highest heaven. He who knows this becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great in offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge; he becomes great in fame. 3.6.1.
Thus ends the sixth section.

One should not criticize food; that is a violation of one's vow. Food is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the body is the eater of food. The body is established in the vital breath, and the vital breath is established in the body. Thus, this food is established in food. He who knows that this food is established in food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame. 3.7.1.
Thus ends the seventh section.

One should not reject food; that is the vow. Water, indeed, is food; light is the eater of food. Light is established in water; water is established in light. Thus, this food is established in food. He who knows this food to be established in food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food, an eater of food, great with offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame. 3.8.1.
Thus ends the eighth section.

One should hold food in high esteem; that is the vow. Earth is indeed food, and space is the eater of food. Space is established upon earth, and earth is established upon space. Thus, this food is established upon food. He who knows that this food is established upon food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great in offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame. 3.9.1.
Thus ends the ninth section.

One should not refuse anyone lodging; that is his vow. Therefore, by whatever means possible, he should obtain much food. They say, "Food has been prepared for him. Indeed, this is food prepared at the beginning; for him, food is prepared at the beginning. Indeed, this is food prepared in the middle; for him, food is prepared in the middle. Indeed, this is food prepared at the end; for him, food is prepared at the end. (3.10.1)

He who knows thus: "Security" is in speech; "acquisition and security" (yogakṣema) is in the out-breath and in-breath; "action" is in the hands; "motion" is in the feet; "liberation" is in the anus—these are the human designations. Now, the divine ones: "Satisfaction" is in rain; "strength" is in lightning. 3.10.2.

"Glory" (yaśas) [is Brahman] in cattle; "light" (jyotis) in the stars; "procreation, immortality, and bliss" (prajātiḥ amṛtam ānandaḥ) in the organ of generation; "the All" (sarvam) in space. One should meditate upon it as the foundation (pratiṣṭhā). One becomes possessed of a foundation. One should meditate upon it as greatness (mahaḥ). One becomes great. One should meditate upon it as mind (manaḥ). One becomes possessed of mind. 3.10.3.

One should venerate that as "the Bowing" (*namas*); desires bow down before him. One should venerate that as "Brahman"; he becomes possessed of Brahman. One should venerate that as "the Death-surrounding of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ parimara*); his enemies and rivals die around him, as do those who are hostile and inimical. That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun are one. 3.10.4.

He who knows this, having departed from this world, having reached this self consisting of food, having reached this self consisting of vital breath, having reached this self consisting of mind, having reached this self consisting of consciousness, and having reached this self consisting of bliss, moves about, eating what he desires and assuming whatever form he desires, through these worlds, singing this Sāman:
"Hā3vu! Hā3vu! Hā3vu! 3.10.5.
I am food, I am food, I am food;
I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food;
I am the maker of fame, I am the maker of fame, I am the maker of fame.
I am the first-born of Truth, prior even to the gods, at the navel of immortality. Whoever gives me away, he indeed possesses me.
I eat the food that eats food;
I have overcome the entire world;
light is like the sun.
Whoever knows thus—this is the Upaniṣad. 3.10.6.
Thus ends the tenth section.
Thus ends the Bhṛgu-vallī.
Thus ends the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
